passages.t: Rabbah falls, while David stays in Jerusalem
passages.happening:
‘In the spring, at the time when kings march out to war, Joab led out the army and ravaged the land of the Ammonites. He came to Rabbah and besieged it, but David remained in Jerusalem. And Joab attacked Rabbah and demolished it’ (verse 1).

David takes the crown from the head of their king, a talent of gold set with precious stones, and it is placed on his own head, and he takes a great amount of plunder (verse 2). ‘David brought out the people who were there and put them to work with saws, iron picks, and axes’ (verse 3), in all the Ammonite cities, and returns to Jerusalem.
passages.hearers:
Spring, after the winter rains, was the normal season for war: roads were passable and armies could live off the ripening crops. Rabbah, the Ammonite capital, stood on the site of modern Amman. A crown weighing a talent, commonly estimated at around thirty kilograms, would have been too heavy to wear for long, and many suggest it was ceremonial or belonged to an idol: the Hebrew for their king, malkam, can also be read as Milcom, the Ammonite god. Putting a defeated king's crown on the victor's head was a public sign that rule had passed to him.

Verse 3 is difficult. The Hebrew verb can be read as sawed, and older translations such as the King James Version said that David cut the people with saws. The parallel in 2 Samuel 12:31 uses a verb meaning to set or put, and most modern translations, the BSB among them, read both passages as forced labor with saws, picks and axes, a common fate for conquered people put to work on royal building.

The chapter draws on 2 Samuel 11:1, 12:26-31 and 21:18-22, and what it leaves out matters as much as what it keeps. See the hard question below.
passages.later: Second Samuel opens the same way: ‘In the spring, at the time when kings march out to war, David sent out Joab and his servants with the whole army of Israel. They destroyed the Ammonites and besieged Rabbah, but David remained in Jerusalem’ (2 Samuel 11:1). There the next verse begins the story of Bathsheba.
passages.hard:
Why does Chronicles leave out David's sin with Bathsheba?

In 2 Samuel the words but David remained in Jerusalem open the story of David's adultery with Bathsheba and the killing of her husband Uriah (2 Samuel 11-12), and the following chapters tell of Absalom's and Sheba's revolts (2 Samuel 13-20). Chronicles uses the same words and moves straight to the fall of Rabbah. Readers account for this in different ways.

Some critics have taken it as an attempt to clean up David's record. Most scholars now read it differently. The Chronicler's first readers already had Samuel and Kings; he was not hiding what they knew. He chose his material to show David as the king who secured Israel and prepared for the temple, and the family tragedies did not serve that purpose. He also does not make David spotless: in the next chapter he tells David's sin in the census at full length, with David's own confession. And he names Uriah the Hittite among the mighty men (11:41), a name no reader could hear without remembering. Chronicles is best read beside Samuel as a second portrait, not as a replacement for it.
passages.asks: The same sentence that opens David's worst sin in 2 Samuel opens a victory here. Ask what you would leave out if you told your own story, and why. And ask whether there is a confession you have avoided by telling only the good chapters.

passages.happening: War breaks out with the Philistines at Gezer, and Sibbecai kills Sippai, a descendant of the Rephaim (verse 4). In another battle ‘Elhanan son of Jair killed Lahmi the brother of Goliath the Gittite, the shaft of whose spear was like a weaver’s beam’ (verse 5). At Gath a huge man with six fingers on each hand and six toes on each foot, also descended from Rapha, taunts Israel, and David's nephew Jonathan kills him (verses 6-7). ‘So these descendants of Rapha in Gath fell at the hands of David and his servants’ (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
These short episodes are undated and may come from different points in David's reign. Gezer and Gath were Philistine or border cities, and Gath was Goliath's home. The Rephaim were remembered in Israel as a people of great stature who lived in Canaan and east of the Jordan before Israel. Scholars differ on whether the term names a people, a clan of warriors, or a category of giants of the past; the text treats these men as formidable enemies who fell to ordinary Israelite soldiers.

The giant at Gath taunted Israel, charaph, the same verb used of Goliath defying the armies of the living God. To taunt Israel was to taunt Israel's God, and in both stories the taunter falls. The pattern is quietly significant. Years before, a young David killed Goliath with God's help; now ordinary soldiers of his army do the same.

Verse 5 has a well-known parallel. The standard Hebrew of 2 Samuel 21:19 says that Elhanan killed Goliath the Gittite, though 1 Samuel 17 gives Goliath to David, and Chronicles says Elhanan killed Lahmi, Goliath's brother. Many scholars think the Samuel text was damaged in copying, and that Chronicles keeps the better reading. Others think Samuel keeps an older tradition that the Chronicler smoothed. Some suggest that Goliath was a name borne by more than one warrior. The site's page on the numbers in Samuel and Chronicles sets out all three, and these notes take no side.
passages.later: When David faced Goliath he said, “You come against me with sword and spear and javelin, but I come against you in the name of the LORD of Hosts, the God of the armies of Israel, whom you have defied” (1 Samuel 17:45).
passages.asks: The courage David once showed alone had spread to the men around him. Ask whose courage has spread to you, and whose faith you are passing on. And ask what giant you have assumed only someone else could face.
